articles.headline: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web
keyFacts: Security firm Censys discovered more than 800 deployments of the Chinese-made Artex AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet without passwords.
Researchers said the open-source penetration testing software has been linked to recent cyberattacks against the Korean finance industry and IT support giant ConnectWise.
Artex announced it would transition to a closed-source model, though copies of its code remain available on code-sharing sites.
body: Security researchers have discovered hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet for anyone to access, potentially allowing outsiders to launch cyberattacks against unsuspecting targets.

The hacking software, called Artex, is an open-source autonomous penetration testing tool, meaning software that automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses, and it’s been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July. As open-source software, it’s free for anyone to download and run on their own servers, making it a popular tool for those who cannot access Anthropic or OpenAI’s most advanced cybersecurity AI models for discovering security vulnerabilities. Microsoft has previously described Artex as a system of AI agents that can conduct cyberattacks “from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction.”

In a blog post, cybersecurity firm Censys, which scans the internet for exposed or vulnerable systems, said that it identified more than 800 distinct deployments of Artex that were accessible from the web without needing a password to log in.

Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at Censys who wrote the blog post, said that not every instance of Artex is operated maliciously and many are used for authorized testers. But it’s unclear why hundreds of these Artex systems are exposed to the web, as the software does not require them to be accessible from the internet.

The findings underscore how even powerful hacking tools can be misconfigured to be publicly accessible by anyone, increasing the chance that someone will find and misuse them. The publicly accessible systems also expose attack tools, such as implants (hidden malicious software) used to compromise and maintain persistent access to a victim’s network.

Security companies have linked the use of Artex to several broad-scale cyberattacks, including against the Korean finance industry in September. Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike attributed the attacks to a Chinese-speaking hacker who used an Artex instance in the attacks, in part because the hacker had left an “open directory” hosting the system. Censys said that its data showed the Artex instance in question had been publicly exposed for months, and appeared to contain more attack data that extended “well beyond South Korean banks,” including payment and gaming companies.

Artex was also used in an attack on IT support giant ConnectWise earlier in October, which allowed Chinese-linked hackers to spy on thousands of organizations whose data and files are hosted in Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft, which has visibility into the attack, said in a blog post that the hackers used Artex to break into customer’s cloud environments and steal their data at such speed that defenders had “little time to detect and respond.”
Many of the attacks linked to Artex involved exploiting simple vulnerabilities, such as guessing weak or known passwords, and a lack of multi-factor authentication.
The findings show that simple vulnerabilities, including misconfigurations, can expose both the attacker and their targets.

Artex has since announced it would go closed-source, effectively limiting further releases for paid customers. There are still dozens of copies of Artex’s code available on code-sharing sites that can still be used in active attacks.

articles.headline: Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
keyFacts: A bipartisan Senate bill aims to speed up energy and data center projects by limiting environmental reviews and legal challenges.
Supporters say the legislation will boost renewable energy, cut emissions, and lower household utility bills.
Environmental advocates warn the bill will weaken public oversight and fast-track polluting fossil fuel projects.
body: A massive permitting bill that could help energy projects come online much quicker and potentially lower utility bills for Americans is advancing with bipartisan support. And while it could be a catalyst for lots of clean energy, it could also speed up polluting projects and limit oversight of new data centers.
Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
The Senate will vote to push through a giant — and controversial — permitting reform bill.
Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
The Senate will vote to push through a giant — and controversial — permitting reform bill.

With data centers demanding more electricity for AI, environmental advocates fear that developers could take advantage of the reforms to evade public scrutiny and rely more heavily on fossil fuels. The bill sacrifices caution for speed, limiting environmental reviews and preventing communities from stopping a project from moving forward by taking it to court.

“Whether it is permits to bulldoze wetlands, the fast-tracking of gas pipelines or general environmental review, with this legislation, data centers would not need to answer to the concerns of local communities,” Christy Goldfuss, executive director of the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), says in an email to The Verge. “People would be shocked to realize their representatives are rushing such a consequential decision.”
The bill sacrifices caution for speed

The sea change in Congress following the midterm elections could put the bill in an even more precarious position, giving Democrats a better shot at pushing for their priorities in the bill and potentially triggering a fight with President Donald Trump. Should it come up for a vote during the current lame-duck session or get kicked to next year, the bill will test whether Democrats and Republicans can actually get something done to address some of the biggest issues voters carried with them to the polls: rising energy costs and data centers encroaching on their communities.
“They swung big with this bill. It’s a really good bipartisan compromise,” Xan Fishman, executive vice president of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, tells The Verge.

Four senators calling themselves the “four corners” — Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) — introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on September 30th. “If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share,” Whitehouse, a climate hawk, said in the press release.

The announcement simultaneously garnered support from climate and renewable energy groups, as well as fossil fuel interests. “Pass the frickin’ bill so we can start building things again,” the US Oil & Gas Association said in a statement.

The Senate could vote to move the bill forward as early as next week, teeing it up for potential passage before the end of the year, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman expects President Trump will want to sign the bill if the current Republican-controlled Congress acts, adding in an email that the White House has been “very involved” in negotiations. Newly empowered Democrats, however, could decide to drag out debate on the bill until next year in order to make fewer concessions to Republicans.
“Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control.”

If it becomes law, the bill would limit the reach of bedrock laws (stemming back to the 1970s environmental movement) that protect water resources and endangered species and give the public an opportunity to weigh in on large projects that might impact public health. Over the years, however, reviews that once took months at most might take several years or even decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman attributes the delays largely to lengthy legal battles. Now, agencies have to spend more time preparing for lawsuits as they consider permitting applications, Fishman says. That holds up development on all kinds of infrastructure projects, including cleaner energy alternatives to fossil fuels.

Fishman expects BAAJA to be very effective in amending outdated permitting rules that have become burdensome to projects across the board, even those that might ultimately have a net positive impact on the environment. “Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control,” he says. “You want to protect the environment, you want to protect people, but you want to get to a yes or no [on a permit application] in a reasonable amount of time and you don’t want to have this endless litigation cycle.”

The bill would set a 45-day deadline for a lead agency to issue a decision on a project after completing an environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). In many cases, NEPA review is the only opportunity for nearby residents to weigh in on large projects that involve the federal government. And it’s been a key tool for opponents to high-profile projects including the Dakota Access and Keystone XL pipelines. BAAJA narrows the scope of projects subject to NEPA, creating exclusions for transmission upgrades and certain pipeline expansions, to name a couple. Many projects receiving federal loans or grants or that have already been through a similar state environmental assessment would no longer trigger NEPA review.

The bill also sets a strict new 150-day limit for anyone to challenge a project in court over alleged violations of NEPA, the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, or National Historic Preservation Act. And BAAJA strips away a court’s ability to halt a project altogether even if it finds that a federal agency violated NEPA; it would simply force the agency to correct any issues.

The Clean Water Act allows the Army Corps of Engineers to issue general permits to projects that discharge dredged material into US waters as long as they’re deemed as having “minimal adverse environmental effects.” BAAJA could make it easier for large projects including data centers to qualify for those permits.

Some environmental groups are concerned that those general permits would take away public participation requirements for individual projects, especially when it comes to data centers that use a lot of water. The proposals in BAAJA amount to “rubber-stamping permits under the Clean Water Act” and “blocking interference from States and Tribes,” according to the environmental organization Earthjustice Action.
“It will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out.”

They’re also concerned that BAAJA aligns with the Trump administration’s push to deregulate industry and weaken environmental protections in order to swiftly build out more data centers and fossil fuel infrastructure to power them. Data center energy demand has led to a surge of new gas projects in the US, and the bipartisan bill could help streamline reviews for new pipelines delivering fuel for data centers.

“One very big reason why passing BAAJA is such a high priority for the gas industry is it will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out,” Earthjustice Action President Abigail Dillen said in a Thursday blog. “BAAJA delivers a precision strike for developers of dirty data centers.”

Long pipeline delays slow data center development, according to energy research firm Wood Mackenzie. Permitting reform could benefit data center developers building out their own gas generation rather than relying solely on the grid, so-called “behind-the-meter” projects, by ending regulatory delays when it comes to connecting pipelines. Reforms would also speed grid-connected gas generation, Wood Mackenzie says in a recent news release.

“I don’t think we’re seeing it as this bill helping one type of technology over the other. I think it clears the way for all technologies to get onto the grid a little quicker,” Siddhant Warrier, research analyst for North American Power for Wood Mackenzie, tells The Verge.

Notably, the bill is supposed to protect bipartisan interests by preventing any single administration from attacking a particular project type — such as the Biden administration attempting to phase down oil and gas in the power sector or the Trump administration issuing stop work orders to wind farms. BAAJA aims to provide “project certainty” by barring federal agencies from canceling or suspending permits they’ve already approved in most cases. It even allows developers to take agencies to court for “disparate treatment” to sue for damages incurred from project delays.

“This part of the legislation could also lead to a slew of industry lawsuits that result in taxpayers paying billions of dollars to private industry,” the NRDC warns in its analysis of the bill. It could also prevent communities from challenging projects, including data centers, that wind up having unforeseen consequences for the environment and public health.

Despite those concerns, the NRDC and other advocacy groups are optimistic about the bill boosting renewable energy and enabling power grid upgrades needed to meet rising demand while keeping costs down.

BAAJA could shorten the time needed to build a new transmission line nearly in half — from 10 years or more to around five or six years, the NRDC estimates. Transmission lines that carry electricity across long distances — key to getting electrons to urban centers from far-flung solar and wind farms — are particularly tricky to build because of the patchwork of permitting processes they’re subject to across different jurisdictions.

Two separate reports project that the permitting bill would increase renewable energy capacity in the US and cut greenhouse gas emissions as a result. It also points to modest reductions in energy costs as a result of BAAJA passing compared to a baseline reflecting the status quo. The average annual cost of producing electricity would fall by as much as 7 percent by 2041, according to modeling by think tank Resources for the Future. Household electricity bills would lower by $50 to $78 per year by 2040, according to an analysis by research firm Rhodium Group. The White House put out its own analysis in October claiming that the average household could see their electricity bills fall by as much as $251 each year as a result of BAAJA.

One of the ways BAAJA aims to keep utility bills from rising is to force data center developers to pay more for transmission costs. Current law prevents utilities from charging them for costs stemming from both new builds and existing infrastructure, which inadvertently shifts costs to other customers to fill in the gap. The bipartisan bill mandates what’s called “and pricing” so that data centers and other large electricity customers would be on the hook to pay for both added and existing infrastructure.

The bill would also require utilities to disclose electricity sales to data centers. It would force large data center developers to make financial assurances to utilities before they break ground, as well as make them responsible for covering costs of new energy projects even if the data center shutters before the infrastructure is paid off.

Unfortunately, the bill may only solve part of the problem since utility rates reflect more than just transmission costs. Increasing electricity demand from the data center boom can still raise prices for fuel and gas turbines, for example. And the bill doesn’t address other issues that have sparked backlash against data centers, like noise and air pollution from generators on site.

Still, without permitting reform, gas and power prices would likely continue to climb as new energy projects keep hitting bottlenecks, according to Wood Mackenzie. Even environmental groups concerned about some of the provisions in BAAJA are holding out to see if Congress can amend the bill to strengthen environmental and consumer protections.

The bill has become a sort of Rorschach test for its backers, one expert speaking on background tells The Verge. They’re all optimistic that their energy source of choice, be it oil and gas or solar and wind, will ultimately come out on top — as long as it gets the green light to build.

articles.headline: Mass Effect-like RPG The Expanse: Osiris Reborn ropes in David Gaider, the original lead writer of Bioware's Dragon Age series
keyFacts: David Gaider is collaborating with Owlcat Games on the narrative for The Expanse: Osiris Reborn.
Gaider announced his involvement on BlueSky while continuing his work at Summerfall Studios.
Owlcat Games recently recast the male protagonist, now voiced by Blythe Melin, following fan feedback.
body: The Expanse: Osiris Reborn looks like it's carrying the best bits of Mass Effect forward, and in an encouraging move, the developers have been collaborating with David Gaider.

Of course, David Gaider is best known as the lead writer on Dragon Age: Origins, Dragon Age 2 and Dragon Age: Inquisition - he's also often credited as the architect of its dark fantasy world Thedas. Gaider's post-BioWare career saw him open his own game development house Summerfall Studios, which most recently released an ambitious roleplaying musical called Stray Gods.
But he's now lending a hand to a game that's not too dissimilar to BioWare's other hugely famous roleplaying series, while still working on his own games at Summerfall.

"Alongside my work at Summerfall, I've also been collaborating with the Owlcat Games team on The Expanse: Osiris Reborn, focusing on certain aspects of the game's narrative. The Expanse has long been one of my favourite series, and so obviously I jumped at the opportunity to be involved," he wrote on BlueSky.

"The Owlcat team has been so great, it's really such a treat. One thing I enjoy is how responsive they are to the fans," Gaider added, pointing to how the studio recently recast the male version of its protagonist in response to feedback. The game's reworked and re-designed Martian Captain is now voiced by Blythe Melin.

The Expanse: Osiris Reborn shouldn't be confused for the other very Mass Effect-y RPG coming out next year, Exodus. Though it's good to hear that both upcoming projects have some BioWare veterans on board, especially after the famed developer was shut down and had its own promising, actual Mass Effect game cancelled.
Bertie enjoyed what he played of the upcoming game in Eurogamer's The Expanse preview, but also had some concerns about the developer's use of generative AI.

body: Fantasy football Week 9 PPR cheat sheet: Jonah Coleman vaults into borderline must-start territory
Dave Richard breaks down every viable starting option across every game using a 1-10 confidence scale to help managers navigate injuries, byes and tricky lineup decisions

Every lineup decision matters as the Fantasy football season approaches its midpoint, and Week 9 presents another challenging slate for managers trying to separate dependable starters from potential disappointments. With several teams on bye, injuries continuing to shake up depth charts and several big-name players facing difficult matchups, knowing who to trust could be the difference between securing a much-needed victory and watching valuable Fantasy points pile up on your bench.
That's where Dave Richard's Week 9 PPR cheat sheet comes in.

What do the numbers mean? All weekly analysis, from data points to matchup outlooks to game-flow predictions, is represented as a number on a 1-10 confidence scale. The higher the number next to a player's name, the more confident I am that you should start him. The numbers are not projections but confidence scores to help you pick who to start. All relevant players for this week are listed, so if you do not see a player's name, do not start him.

To find a specific player, use your search function (CTRL-F on PCs and Command-F on Macs). articles.headline: Why the US midterms sparked an AI stock selloff
keyFacts: Tech stocks fell sharply on the Nasdaq following the Democrats winning full control of Congress in the US midterm elections.
Investors are worried that Democratic opposition to unhindered data centre expansion will lead to stricter regulations and curbs on the AI industry.
Analysts expect traders to become more selective and evaluate whether political shifts will restrict data centre construction and AI technology.
body: - Published
Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?
That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.
The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.
It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's midterm elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.
A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence.
Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have concerned investors. But worries about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.
AI boom
The release of Chat GPT by Open AI in late 2022 is widely seen as having generated massive public and corporate interest in the practical uses of AI. It also sparked a modern-day gold rush.

Investors flocked to put their money into companies producing computer chips and networking infrastructure, building data centres and providing the energy to power them, as well as developing the AI itself. The value of tech companies soared.

The boom continued into this year. Investments in AI are expected to reach $1trillion in 2026 alone according to research by Goldman Sachs. The sector has scooped up so much available cash that other industries have seen their own borrowing costs increase as a result.
But investors want returns, and in recent months concerns have been growing about whether the AI boom can produce the expected riches.

Those worries have emerged at a time when public comments from AI researchers casting doubt over the safety of artificial intelligence - even suggesting it could represent an existential threat to humanity - have been grabbing headlines and fuelling speculation that a clampdown could lie ahead.
Democrat opposition

While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.

These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills â as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.
A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.
James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to respond to this scepticism.
"While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said.
"We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."

With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.
Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.
The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.
Where next for stocks?

As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.

The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the midterm results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.
The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.

Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.
She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.
Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic".
"There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".

articles.headline: Player-coach rift report will only galvanise England - George
keyFacts: England hooker Jamie George said the squad was upset by a newspaper report claiming player unrest over head coach Steve Borthwick's leadership.
George stated the article was untrue and intended to be divisive, but would instead galvanise the team ahead of their match.
England meet Australia in the Nations Championship on Sunday at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham.
body: - Published
England hooker Jamie George says the squad are "really upset" by a newspaper article claiming the end of their summer tour was marked by player unrest over head coach Steve Borthwick's leadership.
A report in the Times, external says unhappy players wanted summit talks with Borthwick and Rugby Football Union chief executive Bill Sweeney in Argentina in July.

It alleges there are disagreements among Borthwick's wider coaching group, which has been subject to frequent change in his nearly four years in charge, and concerns over the head coach's man-management skills.
England meet Australia in the Nations Championship on Sunday at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham, with George querying the timing of the article as well as its contents.
The Saracens hooker, who was made England captain by Borthwick in 2024 before the role passed to Maro Itoje 12 months later, said that he did not recognise the situation described by the article.
"I can tell you that a lot of it's untrue," George told Rugby Union Weekly.
"We, as a squad, are incredibly disappointed by it.
"You just have to look at the timing of the article - two days out from our first Test match. I think it's clearly there to try and be divisive.
"It is the first time I think in my England career that as a group we've had to address an article that's been written, but we spoke about it brilliantly.
"Maro called a leader's meeting and thought that that was the best way of us going about it.
"Whoever's written this article, obviously their aim was for it to be divisive. Unfortunately for them, it's going to go the other way.

"This is going to galvanise us, it's going to make us tighter. We speak a lot about standing up for people, we speak a lot about helping each other, and we've got to make sure that we do that for Steve.
"He has had a bit of a personal attack here and an unwarranted one at that."
While none of the sources for the Times article were directly quoted in it, some of those previously involved in Borthwick's regime have criticised the set-up.

England's most-capped men's player Ben Youngs, who won the Premiership under Borthwick at Leicester and was part of his England squad at the 2023 Rugby World Cup, has described how he felt the head coach failed to offer sympathy and support when his family was affected by a terminal illness., external

Defence coach Felix Jones helped South Africa to back-to-back world titles, but lasted only seven months working under Borthwick before an "unstable working environment" reportedly motivated him to hand in his notice.

"The depiction is not something I recognise," Borthwick told Rugby Union Weekly of the Times article, emphasising that meetings between senior players and coaches are a feature of most coaching set-ups.
"As senior players part of our job is to challenge Steve," added George. "Steve is so open to us giving feedback and having challenge.
"It is very much a two-way conversation and that was definitely there in Argentina.
"There was an edge to what we were doing - there was plenty going on - but at no stage was it toxic.
"I don't know many organisations in the world that don't review big tournaments and try and make sure you take plenty of learnings."
England's autumn campaign begins against Australia on Sunday.
Borthwick will be acutely aware that it was at the same point in the World Cup cycle that his predecessor Eddie Jones was sacked.

The Australian, who, like Borthwick, had been heavily backed by the RFU, was eventually forced out after a November 2022 defeat by South Africa was met by a chorus of jeers from the Twickenham stands.
Allianz Stadium generates about 90% of the RFU's revenue, the vast majority of which comes via men's national team matchdays.
England's meeting with the Wallabies will be the first time Borthwick's team have returned to the venue since February's 42-21 loss to Ireland in a miserable Six Nations campaign.
While wins over Fiji and Argentina in their last two outings have ended a run of five straight losses, England's winning percentage for 2026 is still only 38%.
Only two years since the start of the Millennium have ended with a worse return.
After taking over from Jones, Borthwick very nearly led England to the Rugby World Cup final less than a year later, losing to South Africa by a single point in their semi-final.
His 2025 campaign fuelled hope with 11 wins from 12 matches, including a rare victory over New Zealand.
However, the momentum gathered on that run has evaporated.
The All Blacks, rejuvenated under new coach Dave Rennie, loom two weeks after Sunday's meeting with Australia, with a match against Japan, now led by Jones himself, in between.

articles.headline: The folks behind John Wick are back with Karōshi trailer
keyFacts: Lionsgate released a trailer for the new dystopian action-thriller film Karoshi, created by John Wick director Chad Stahelski and writer-director Takashi Doscher.
The film is set in a futuristic corporate Manhattan at a company called Ikigai Technologies, following an outsider seeking vengeance after a worker dies.
The movie stars Teo Yoo, Takehiro Hira, Giancarlo Esposito, Cynthia Erivo, Bill Camp, Richard Harmon, Isabel May, and Show Kasamatsu, with release planned for early next year.
body: Those of us missing the John Wick universe can take heart, because Chad Stahelski—who created that franchise—is coming back early next year with a new dystopian action film. It's called Karōshi (a Japanese term that means "death overwork"), and Lionsgate released a killer trailer that puts this film at the top of my list of "must see" movies of 2027.

Dying from working too hard is a very real phenomenon, not just in Japan and much of Asia, but also in Sweden, where some 700 workers die each year from overwork. The physical cause is usually stress-related heart attacks or strokes, as well as suicide ( karōjisatsu in Japan). Writer/director Takashi Doscher has transported that concept to a grim, futuristic corporate Manhattan, specifically a company called Ikigai Technologies. Per the official premise:

Karōshi is an action-thriller set in a near-future Manhattan, where corporate loyalty and cultural tradition have reshaped everyday life. When a mysterious outsider infiltrates a powerful company after a worker’s death, he exposes the violent system hidden beneath its polished surface.

Teo Yoo ( Past Lives ) stars as the aptly named Hiro, who is clearly out for vengeance against the offending corporation. The cast also includes Takehiro Hira, so memorable in the 2024 miniseries Shōgun , as well as Giancarlo Esposito, Cynthia Erivo, Bill Camp, Richard Harmon, Isabel May, and Show Kasamatsu.

articles.headline: Los Angeles is about to test a new kind of housing politics
keyFacts: Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass lost her reelection bid to Nithya Raman after undermining affordable housing policies and fighting state efforts to increase housing production.
During her term, Bass weakened her fast-track housing executive order, opposed a state law requiring denser housing near transit, and banned density-increasing applications in fire-damaged areas.
Raman has promised to break from Bass's approach, making her upcoming mayoralty a test for whether sprawling American cities can build their way out of housing shortages.
body: Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman at an election night party, November 3, 2026. | Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images

It’s notoriously hard to govern Los Angeles, a city that gives its mayor less direct authority over the government than in a city like New York or Chicago. But even so, it’d be hard to do much worse than Karen Bass.

Elected mayor of LA in 2022, Bass campaigned on promises to solve the city’s homelessness and housing affordability crises (which are really part of the same underlying crisis ). She then spent her term undermining her own administration’s affordable housing policy and fighting the state of California’s efforts to compel cities to allow more housing production. She lost her bid for reelection this week to Nithya Raman, an LA City Council member, rising progressive star, and nationally prominent YIMBY.

Los Angeles has the highest ratio of home price to household income of any large city in America, and the second fewest homes per adult of any major city. It has a highly suburbanized and car-oriented fabric, like much of the rest of the country — all of which makes it a kind of proving ground for whether America’s sprawling cities can build their way out of their housing shortages.

Everyone in the city’s political leadership notionally agrees that LA needs to permit a lot more homes to meet demand — the only true way to make housing affordable — but not all of them have evidently had the policy discipline to follow through.

Raman may be different. She has gained a following in housing reform circles over the last few years with her brisk, direct-to-camera social videos explaining how LA’s housing shortage drives up rents and criticizing city policies that make it so difficult to build more homes (perhaps it’s no surprise that she has plenty of friends in Hollywood ).

“There has been an overall lack of urgency in addressing housing supply in [Bass’s] administration,” Raman told me in an interview in July. How best to accommodate LA’s need for more housing, she said, is “a question that the city has actually turned away from.”

Even given LA’s relatively weak mayoralty, Bass’s failures on housing were often a matter of political choice. As The Atlantic’s Marc Novicoff put it , “Bass seems to have gone out of her way to exercise as little power as possible.” Where she did go out of her way to wield her influence, it was often to stop denser housing from being built. Some of her bewildering housing policy choices while in office include:

Days into her term, Bass signed her first executive order, known as ED1, to fast-track housing developments where 100 percent of the apartments are affordable. Applications for these projects were to get approvals within 60 days instead of being dragged through excruciating permitting processes. It was a good idea — and it seemed to be working, quickly attracting developer applications to build thousands of affordable apartments. It was working so well, in fact, that a backlash from vocal NIMBYs followed. Less than six months after signing ED1, in June 2023, Bass weakened it to exclude projects in single-family neighborhoods — which make up three-quarters of LA’s residential land — from the fast-track approval process. Her administration even tried to apply that restriction retroactively to developments that had already applied to build in single-family areas under ED1, a breathtaking display of bureaucratic dysfunction; a judge later ruled that this violated California law. Bass has since added more restrictions to the ED1, and one observer has described it as “functionally gutted” for many developers. To be fair to Bass, even after she weakened it, the program has still resulted in more than 7,700 affordable apartments under construction, according to her campaign.

Bass opposed SB 79, a landmark California law that passed in 2025 requiring cities and suburbs to allow construction of denser housing near transit stops. Permitting apartments near public transit is one of the most basic principles of sensible urban planning. But in LA, it was controversial enough that Bass urged Gov. Gavin Newsom to veto it. After he signed SB 79 into law anyway, Bass worked with LA’s city council to delay much of the law’s most ambitious upzoning until 2030, while permitting smaller apartment buildings near some transit stops.

After the devastating January 2025 fires, some property owners whose homes had burned down in the Pacific Palisades had applied to rebuild under SB 9, another important California law that allows single-family lots to be modestly densified into up to four housing units. In response to backlash from some neighbors , Bass reportedly pressed Newsom to restrict SB 9 in fire-damaged areas; she then banned SB 9 applications in parts of the Palisades. (There are certainly legitimate questions about whether rebuilding in such a fire-prone area is a good idea at all. But Bass offered no publicly available analysis that the modest increase in density allowed by SB 9 posed a special danger, even as she worked to accelerate the rebuilding of single-family homes.)

All of these point to a leader who is not serious about changing the conditions that led to LA’s housing shortage, and lacks the courage to take on what is arguably the city’s most defining political challenge.

Raman has promised to fundamentally break from that approach. That will make her mayoralty an important experiment for the rest of the country. Even modest progress in a city as resistant to housing as LA could help crack open a way forward for new approaches to housing in the many other cities that face affordability crises.

This won’t be easy for her — she’ll face the same anti-building political pressures, and will need to maintain a cooperative relationship with the city council. When I spoke to Raman over the summer, I noticed that she treaded gingerly around the topic of adding density to single-family neighborhoods. Because of the uniquely American obsession with keeping single-family homes segregated from other types of development, it can be a real political third rail in LA and nationwide. But research has suggested the city can’t fill its housing shortage without building more in those neighborhoods. Raman will, at least, have an important ally in California’s newly elected governor, Xavier Becerra, who is also a strong YIMBY.

Raman’s affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) makes her emblematic of a fusion that’s been emerging in Democratic politics, between supply-side abundance and left-wing economic populism. It’s also evident in politicians like Zohran Mamdani and some of the young Democrats who won elections across the country this week.
I think this is right.
It's not just that Talarico (et al) combines elements of left populism, abundance pragmatism, and cultural moderation. It's also that the definitions of "left" and "moderate" are in flux.
Take "left." Talarico's all-of-the-above position on energy, eg,… https://t.co/elbUP9vT11
— Derek Thompson (@DKThomp) November 5, 2026

From talking to Raman, I have the sense that she’s more at home with the YIMBY part of her politics than the DSA part. Her relationship with the DSA’s LA chapter has been strained (though it did endorse her candidacy). But her social-democratic commitments are also sincere — she’s been a strong champion of rent control and tenant protections in LA, for example, and helped shape a stronger rent stabilization law the city adopted last year.

The new political syntheses taking shape on the American left are exciting and intriguing. Whether it will finally make a breakthrough in LA’s — and California’s, and America’s — housing crisis, of course, remains to be tested. But it’s a welcome sign that American politics need not remain trapped in the same orthodoxies and failures.

articles.headline: OpenAI and Anthropic Drop New AI Tools for Cybersecurity, Images and Finance
keyFacts: OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Cyber, a new security-focused model restricted to cybersecurity experts in the Daybreak program.
OpenAI updated ChatGPT Images 2.6 to be fifty percent faster and capable of generating animated GIFs for all users globally.
Anthropic partnered with Plaid to allow US paying subscribers to connect financial accounts to the Claude chatbot for spending analysis.
body: Every week is a busy week in the artificial intelligence industry, and this week is no exception. As voters expressed serious concerns about AI and data centers at the ballot box, OpenAI and Anthropic — makers of ChatGPT and Claude, respectively — each dropped new updates to make their chatbots a little more capable.

All these changes come amid rapidly changing government and financial environments. The midterm elections, in which Democrats handily beat Republican candidates across the country, showed that anti-AI and anti-Big Tech campaigns resonated with voters. Tech critics told CNET this week that there is a clear desire for government officials at every level to change how they interact with technology companies — to keep their campaign promises. The election results are also shaking up Wall Street, as investors’ fears about AI’s long-term financial viability grow.

Smaller updates like these are helpful for everyday AI users, and there’s a benefit for AI companies, too. They can prove they’re competitive in a market that is losing confidence in AI. Here are the three biggest AI updates to ChatGPT and Claude.
More from CNET
GPT-6 Cyber: Another AI model you can’t use yet

Gone are the days when every new AI tool got an immediate general release — and that’s probably for the best. Now, when a major AI lab has a new frontier AI model, it slow-rolls its access, and it starts with cybersecurity defenders. That’s exactly what OpenAI did with its newest model variant, GPT-6 Cyber.

GPT-6 Cyber is a version of OpenAI’s newest flagship model that’s specifically made for security research and work. OpenAI says it’s best at finding vulnerabilities and staying in its secure container. Those two things matter a lot. Earlier this fall, an OpenAI model was partially responsible for helping researchers identify a major vulnerability in PHP, a programming language that’s used in the majority of websites. And any improvements to keep AI secure are necessary. We saw many instances this summer of AI agents breaking out of their testing environments and making cybersecurity experts fear future autonomous hacks.
You won’t be able to use GPT-6 Cyber unless you’re a cybersecurity expert who’s part of OpenAI’s Daybreak program. Cisco and Mozilla teams are already using the model, according to OpenAI.
ChatGPT gets into animated GIFs

OpenAI also added a minor model update to its AI image model, called ChatGPT Images 2.6. The biggest improvement is its speed; OpenAI says the new model is 50% faster than before. That matters for AI enthusiasts who are generating multiple variations of a prompt. The new model also lets you animate your AI images into short GIFs. It’s available globally now for all ChatGPT users.

This isn’t the return of the long-dead Sora AI video model, but it is a sign that OpenAI isn’t giving up on the creative AI space entirely. Anthropic, by comparison, has never had a traditional AI image or video generator and opted for a design tool that’s better suited for mocking up websites and apps.
Claude wants to see your money
Anthropic is teaming up with fintech platform Plaid to help you bring your financial information into its Claude chatbot.

The idea is that if you connect your financial accounts with the chatbot, like a credit card, Claude can help you understand your spending and plan to meet savings goals. So you could connect your checking and savings accounts and ask Claude to analyze your spending habits. It can’t make changes to your accounts, like moving your money around, and Anthropic says it doesn’t train its models based on your financial chats. It’s a beta feature only available in the US for paying subscribers.

Both companies say they have strong security measures in place to keep your information safe. But CNET always recommends a cautious approach when it comes to sharing your financial information (or any sensitive information) with an AI product.
(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

articles.headline: Trump names Stephen Miller new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
keyFacts: President Donald Trump named Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff to replace Susie Wiles.
Miller will take over the role on Monday, while Wiles transitions to Trump's political operation.
A current White House official stated that Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday night and the decision was amicable.
body: President Donald Trump has named Stephen Miller his new White House chief of staff, calling him one of his "most trusted advisors."
Miller will ascend to the role on Monday, officially replacing Susie Wiles, who Trump said will be moving to his political operation.
"I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!" Trump wrote.
Moments after Trump's announcement, Wiles issued a statement of her own.
"Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff," Wiles said.

"Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First," she added. "More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will."

The announcement came after Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections, dealing a major blow to President Donald Trump after the war with Iran and persistent affordability concerns loomed large over elections, as voters weighed the economic toll of the conflict.
A current White House official told Fox News Digital the decision was "very amicable" and Wiles handed her resignation in Thursday night.

Wiles worked on Trump’s 2016 and 2020 campaigns, making history as the first woman to serve as chief of staff. She is a longtime Trump ally, first throwing her support behind him in 2015 when she became the Trump campaign's co-chairwoman in Florida.

"As a card-carrying member of the G.O.P. establishment, many thought my full-throated endorsement of the Trump candidacy was ill-advised — even crazy," Wiles told the New York Times in a rare public statement back in 2016.

Wiles has served in her role for 21 months, making her Trump’s longest-serving chief of staff across both of his terms. Trump cycled through four chiefs of staff during his first term, with John Kelly serving the longest—about 17 months.
She has been dubbed the "Ice Maiden" by Trump, which he noted in his 2024 victory speech, for hard-nosed approach to handling business.
Wiles was seen as Trump’s behind-the-scenes, sitting in on high-level meetings and standing by his side at events, but Wiles rarely spoke directly to the public.
In March, Wiles announced she had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer upon early detection and received a strong prognosis. Six months later in September, she shared she was cancer free.

"With grit, determination, faith and the support of extraordinary people, it is possible to fight this disease while continuing to embrace the work, relationships and sense of purpose that make you who you are," Wile wrote in a USA Today op-ed in September. "For me, that means serving my president and my country. I will always be grateful to President Donald Trump for the kindness and compassion while I was undergoing treatment."

articles.headline: Xbox Series X | X25 Special Edition Console – Invite Requests Are Up at Amazon
keyFacts: Amazon is allowing customers to request an invite to purchase the translucent green Xbox Series X | X25 Special Edition console.
The 25th-anniversary console costs $909.23, is limited to 25,000 numbered units, and will release on November 13.
Amazon stated that requesting an invite does not guarantee a purchase opportunity and not all requests will be granted.
body: Back in August, when preorders went up for the translucent green Xbox Series X | X25 Special Edition console, they sold out almost instantly. That was a bummer for longtime Xbox fans who wanted to get their hands on one of these limited-edition 25th-anniversary consoles. Now you have another chance, thanks to Amazon. Instead of doing preorders on a first-come-first-served basis, Amazon is letting anyone interested request an invite to buy this special-edition Xbox (you can request one here ).
Xbox Series X - X25 Limited Edition Invite Request

Requesting an invite doesn’t mean you’ll necessarily end up being invited to buy a console. But it gives you a chance to be invited, which is better than nothing. As Amazon says, “If invited to purchase, you’ll get an email when the item is available. Not all requests will be granted.”

The console is meant to celebrate the 25th anniversary of Xbox. It’s set to release on November 13 and costs (the curiously specific price) $909.23. Only 25,000 numbered consoles are being manufactured, which explains the difficulty people have had securing a preorder.

So what do you get if you do end up buying it? You get a 1TB Xbox Series X console, decked out in translucent green. The front of the console has an X25 logo, and when you turn it on, the X logo glows green as well. You also get a matching controller (which is also sold separately, and is still available at some retailers). Finally, you get a digital copy of Halo: Campaign Evolved, a remake of the campaign from the original Halo (see our review ).
XBOX Wireless Controller X25 Special Edition (Available Now)

Overall, this has been an extremely popular item among IGN readers. It’s a great-looking piece of hardware that celebrates 25 years since the original Xbox hit store shelves. If you want one, or even if you might be interested in one, there’s no reason not to request an invite.

articles.headline: It's hard to meet women when I keep teleporting all the time
keyFacts: Josh used the Anoxic Dating mod in GTA 5 to simulate relationships and eventually marry an in-game NPC.
The author used repeated dialogue prompts and teleportation abilities to navigate the dating process and secure a spouse.
The author plans to continue modding GTA 5 daily to either recreate GTA 6 elements or break the game.
body: I'm modding GTA 5 every day in a quest to either transform it into a PC version of GTA 6 or break it entirely. Come back tomorrow to find out what new horrible thing I've done to Rockstar's baby, or check out what I got up to earlier.

Am I cheating? I might be cheating. I did not actually install a new mod for today's iteration of Los Santos Customs. Like I mentioned yesterday, updating my Script Hook thing seems to have breathed life into a host of old mods I'd installed, but which did not work. Now they work, and here we are.

I'm definitely not cheating on my wife though. I have a wife now, by the way, and all I had to do to get her was teleport her to the roof of a skyscraper and gift her 22 sports cars. No more lonely nights for me, and it's all thanks to Dating Simulator (Public Beta), a mod we probably shouldn't look too deep into in case it gets weird.

Dating Simulator—which refers to itself as Anoxic Dating in the in-game menus—brings the experience of real-life dating into GTA 5. You approach women on the street, ask them how they are 40 times, and then they give you their number. This makes you "Friends" according to the mod's hierarchy of romance, unlocking new, vaguely more intimate dialogue. Discuss the weather with your muse 50 times, then tell her you miss her 60 times and, brother, you're well on the way to wife town.
You can't go through this process with men because it would, obviously, be weird to say "Tell me about your interests" to a man 37 times in a row.

Anyway, I'm basically the most charming man on Earth, but my attempts to corral a woman into marriage were hampered somewhat by my tendency to teleport to random spots on the map every 50 seconds. Fortunately, Anoxic Dating lets you teleport your girlfriends to wherever you are. "How are you?" I'd ask several hundred times, then teleport, then summon my new friend, and say "Crazy weather we're having, huh?" another hundred times. In this way I made her fall for me.

It culminated on the roof of a skyscraper. There I was, there we were, and in line with tradition I kept saying "Will you marry me?" over and over again. She didn't bite, though, and my teleport timer was ticking down. I did what any man would do: immediately bought her 22 sports cars at $45,000 each. I forget her name, but she is now my wife. We are very happy.

articles.headline: Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature – what to expect
keyFacts: Google is rolling out a "Notify when left behind" feature to its Find My hub for Android devices.
According to 9to5Google, the feature alerts users when registered devices are separated from their phones at unsaved locations.
The feature currently works only with specific Bluetooth trackers like Chipolo and Moto Tag, notifying users when items are left away from their registered home address.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- “Notify when left behind” appears in Google’s Find Hub.
- It notifies you when registered devices are left at an unsaved location.
- The feature is limited right now, but it’s a welcome update.

A much-needed update — “Notify when left behind” — is rolling out to Google’s Find My hub. The feature sends a notification when a registered device is separated from your phone, except when you leave it at your house.
According to 9to5Google, this feature was first previewed in October, with the notification available for Chipolo trackers and Moto Tag.
More from ZDNET
‘Notify’ finally comes to Android

“Notify when left behind” is my all-time favorite device tracking feature on iOS. Any device set up on my Find My network is compatible with this feature, including my MacBook Air, AirPods Pro 3, and Apple Watch, three devices I often take out of the house — and have indeed left behind once or twice.

If these devices are separated from my phone in an unsaved location, I’ll get a notification of which device I left and where. In iOS, you can customize which locations are “safe,” and won’t notify you if you leave them there.

On Android, this feature is currently limited to only notifying you when a device is left at a location other than the home address registered to your Google account. Hopefully, location customization is on the horizon.
How to enable the feature

Right now, this feature appears to be limited to specific Bluetooth trackers. Photos shared by 9to5Google show compatible trackers have a “Notify when left behind” tab at the bottom of their menu in the Find Hub, so it’s expected that future supported devices will operate the same way.

9to5Google reports that previous updates to Google Play Services indicated this feature’s existence. According to 9to5Google, “Notify when left behind” should be a feature that users can enable when registering a new device with their Find Hub.
Once Google matures and fully rolls out this feature, there should be a setting inside the Find Hub to enable these notifications on every device in your hub.
Android’s advantage over Apple

Android’s breadth of compatibility with third-party manufacturers is its most significant advantage over Apple. Regarding device tracking, you can add Sony headphones, Motorola trackers, and Samsung Galaxy smartwatches to the same Find Hub.

However, my Beats headphones that appear in my Find My hub are not currently supported by this new feature. If Google can expand this feature to all Fast Pair-compatible devices, such as Bluetooth trackers, headphones, smartwatches, laptops, and more, it’ll be easier for consumers to keep tabs on their ever-growing armory of devices.

articles.headline: Fox wraps up its $22 billion Roku deal
keyFacts: Fox Corporation officially completed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku after receiving clearance from the Trump Justice Department.
Roku founder Anthony Wood will join the Fox board to co-lead a new division called Fox Digital Platforms.
Fox stated that Roku will remain an open platform, though the future impact on the service remains unclear.
body: Fox wraps up its $22 billion Roku deal
No Hannity on your home screen, at least for now.

Days after American voters soundly rejected the narratives sold by the Fox Corporation's "news" division, the company has expanded its digital empire. It's now officially the owner of Roku, in a $22 billion deal announced in June. The five-month turnaround is unusually short for a merger of this size, but the Trump Justice Department cleared it nonetheless following a review.

Roku reaches over 100 million households globally, serving as a gateway to streaming platforms like Netflix, YouTube TV and Disney+. It also sells ads and subscription bundles, while owning another streaming service, Tubi. Ironically, Fox sold its Roku shares in 2020 to help fund its Tubi acquisition.

The closure follows reports that Fox News' viewership dropped 27 percent year over year in October. By comparison, CNN's viewership grew by 3 percent and MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) rose by 16 percent. However, Fox News' viewership is still higher than CNN and MS NOW's combined.
Roku founder Anthony Wood will join Fox's board. He'll co-lead Fox Digital Platforms, a new division overseeing Roku, Tubi, Fox One and other digital brands.

What this means for Roku owners isn't yet clear. But given the media empire's inclination toward right-wing politics, it's hard to imagine the company passing up the opportunity to deploy Roku as another megaphone. For what it's worth, Fox says Roku will remain an "open platform" for every content partner. However, the worry is less about what services the company removes and more about what gets promoted on the home screen.

articles.headline: Lauren Boebert's Campaign Hints At Fraud In Her Election Results
keyFacts: Representative Lauren Boebert trailed Democrat Eileen Laubacher by less than 3,000 votes in her midterm election race.
Scott Gessler, a lawyer for Boebert's campaign, said they are investigating unusual voting patterns and expect a recount.
The campaign stated it will continue investigating to ensure every legal vote is counted as outstanding votes remain.
body: Once an election denier, always an election denier?

Rep Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), who proudly backed Donald Trump’s lie that the 2020 election was stolen from him, hinted at wrongdoing this week in the vote tally of her own midterm election race. The counting remained in progress as of this writing.
Scott Gessler, a lawyer for her campaign, said in a news release Thursday, “We are investigating some very unusual voting patterns and expect this election to head to a recount, one way or another.”

“Every legal vote must be counted accurately, fully, and transparently,” he continued. “We will continue to investigate throughout the process to protect the integrity of this election and ensure Coloradans can have complete confidence in the results.”
Gessler noted that “a significant number of votes remain outstanding in the race. “

“We are fighting for every vote and will continue to ensure every legal vote is counted,” he added. “Since election night, ballot returns have been trending in Congresswoman Boebert’s direction, consistently lowering the margin under one percentage point.”
As of Thursday night, Boebert trailed Democrat Eileen Laubacher by less than 3,000 votes in the 4th District ― a deficit of 1.2%.
Boebert sounded a bit more accepting about the possibility of a defeat in a recent interview.
“This doesn’t define me,” she said. “I’m a mom. I’m a granny, and I’m a believer. We’re going to continue moving faith to faith and glory to glory.”
Boebert, who switched districts amid her tenure on Capitol Hill, is seeking her fourth term.
Once considered a strident MAGA disciple of Trump, she has clashed with him on matters such as the Epstein files and the war against Iran.
